advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Fix `store_copy_entries` stride so the slice spans full history even when `len(canonical)` is between `limit` and `2*limit` (e.g. index by `i*len//limit` instead of Python slice stride).
evidence: _dc_fixtures.py:67-69: `if limit > 0 and len(canonical) > limit:` / `stride = len(canonical) // limit` / `canonical = canonical[::stride][:limit]`
For len(canonical)=250, limit=200: stride = 250//200 = 1, so `canonical[::1][:200]` is the oldest 200 sorted ids — a contiguous head slice, not a span.

The span test only uses limit=10 against 1000 ids (stride=100): tests/unit/test_dc_store_copy_bounded_25e0.py `test_the_slice_spans_the_whole_store_rather_than_one_contiguous_era` never exercises the near-limit regime.
advisory.finding: The stride sampling in `store_copy_entries` degrades to a head slice (oldest N tickets) whenever `limit < len(canonical) < 2*limit`: `stride = len(canonical) // limit` yields 1, so `canonical[::1][:limit]` returns the first `limit` sorted entries rather than an even span. This contradicts the docstring/PR claim that the slice 'spans the store's whole history rather than one contiguous era'.
scenarios: A live store with between 201 and 399 canonical tickets copies only the oldest 200, silently narrowing rehearsal coverage to one era.
As the store grows just past the limit, coverage regresses to the very failure mode the docstring says stride sampling prevents.
advisory.suggested_fix: Select via evenly spaced indices: `canonical = [canonical[i * len(canonical) // limit] for i in range(limit)]` when `len(canonical) > limit`.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Drain git archive's stderr concurrently (e.g. capture via a thread or redirect to a temp file) to avoid a stderr-pipe-full deadlock while tar consumes stdout.
evidence: _dc_fixtures.py:80-95: `subprocess.Popen([... git archive ...], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)` then tar consumes stdout, and only after `archive.wait()` is `archive.stderr.read()` called
stderr is never read until after wait(); a large stderr from git can fill the pipe and block the git process while the parent is blocked in `subprocess.run(tar, ...)`.
advisory.finding: In `extract_store_snapshot`, git's stderr is a PIPE that is only drained after `archive.wait()`, while its stdout is streamed to tar concurrently. If git archive writes more than the OS pipe buffer (~64KB) to stderr before tar finishes consuming stdout, git blocks writing to stderr while tar/parent are not reading it, risking a deadlock.
scenarios: git archive emits voluminous warnings (e.g. many pathspec/attribute warnings) to stderr on a large slice, filling the 64KB stderr pipe buffer before tar drains stdout.
advisory.suggested_fix: Redirect archive stderr to a temp file (or a reader thread) instead of an unread PIPE, then read it after wait().

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm canonical ids are always lowercase hex (or make `CANONICAL_ID_RE` case-insensitive) so no id escapes the sampling cap.
evidence: `fullmatch` is used at lines 65-66; an uppercase-hex id would fall into `carried` and bypass the cap.
advisory.finding: `CANONICAL_ID_RE` matches only lowercase hex (`[0-9a-f]`), so a canonical id containing uppercase hex would be misclassified as a bridge-named directory and carried unthinned rather than sampled. This is likely benign given lowercase id convention but is an undocumented assumption not asserted anywhere.
scenarios: A store entry with uppercase-hex canonical id (if ids are ever emitted uppercase) escapes the size cap and inflates the copy.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the AST/text assertions in test_the_snapshot_is_not_buffered_whole_in_memory with a behavioral check of streaming (or drop the structural grep as a change-detector).
evidence: `assert not archives, "git archive is invoked as a list of argv parts, not a shell string"`
_FIXTURES points at tests/external/live_jira_dc/_dc_fixtures.py, which is the executable source under test, not an instruction artifact
advisory.finding: test_the_snapshot_is_not_buffered_whole_in_memory asserts over the AST/text of the source under test (_dc_fixtures.py) — presence of 'subprocess.Popen', absence of a 'git archive' string constant, absence of a tar call with an input= kwarg — rather than any observable behavior. It is a source-grepping change-detector: a behavior-preserving refactor (factoring the streaming pipe into a helper, or streaming via a different constant-memory mechanism) breaks it while the memory guarantee still holds.
scenarios: extract_store_snapshot refactored to stream via a helper or a different constant-memory approach — behavior preserved, test fails

evidence: `assert "reclaim(work)" in source, f"{fixture_file} never reclaims its store copy"`
`assert "yield work" in source, f"{fixture_file} cannot reclaim: it returns instead of yielding"`
`assert shared == local, f"ticket-entry rules diverged: {shared!r} vs {local!r}"`

advisory.finding: test_every_store_copy_fixture_reclaims_its_tree greps the source under test (fixture files) for the literal substrings 'reclaim(work)' and 'yield work' as its pass/fail signal. This is source-grepping over source code under test: renaming the local variable `work`, or implementing teardown via try/finally rather than a bare yield-then-reclaim, preserves behavior but fails the test.
merged_from: test_the_local_ticket_entry_rule_matches_the_harnesss_own compares the ast.unparse'd return expression of _dc_fixtures._is_ticket_entry against _dc_support.is_ticket_entry for exact string equality. Two behaviorally identical predicates written differently (e.g. `not name.startswith('.')` vs `name[:1] != '.'`) would fail this test, so it is a change-detector tied to the exact source text rather than to the equivalence of the two rules.
scenarios: fixture teardown refactored to try/finally or the copy var renamed — behavior preserved, test fails
